title: Building a Vietnamese dialogue system before LLMs
summary: Intent classification, rule-based information extraction, conversation state and structured replies in a historical Vietnamese Covid-19 consultation chatbot, read directly from the repository.
lead: This was an earlier Vietnamese NLP project in a narrow domain: a consultation chatbot for COVID-19 patients. The engineering problem was to understand what a user asked, remember what they said in earlier turns and return a reply through a chat interface. This write-up is a technical retrospective based on the public repository. It is not medical guidance, and no clinical validation, accuracy figure or deployment scale is claimed.

sections.title: Context and scope
paragraphs: The project is the repository minhbtrc/covid-consultant-chatbot. Its commits run from September 2021 to March 2023 across five branches (main, minh, minhbtc, refactor and thang) and come from several author names. My portfolio entry describes this as a project I led, but the repository does not show who did which part, so I describe what the code does and not who wrote each piece.

The bot answers in Vietnamese and covers four scenarios: a short question flow that starts when a user mentions symptoms, answers to general questions about the disease, contact information for local health stations, and current case numbers. Everything else falls back to a default question.
I read the code on the main branch and, where main is incomplete, the other branches. Where a claim could not be checked against code or data, I say so below.

definitions.text: The kind of message: a greeting, a request, information given by the user, or an acknowledgement. Requests carry a sub-intent such as a question about symptoms or contacts.
A piece of information found in the text: age, sex, district, symptoms.
The stored state of the conversation. The code keeps personal information, symptoms, history, a diagnosis record and the current answer choices in one dictionary.
The dialogue manager returns a code naming the next action, such as asking for a district, instead of returning text. The generation stage turns codes into sentences.

sections.title: Split understanding, dialogue and generation
paragraphs: The backend separates natural language understanding, dialogue management and response generation. A message enters through a FastAPI endpoint, /api/send-message, which expects a sender identifier, a message identifier and the text. The bot loads earlier context, extracts intent and entities, passes the results to the dialogue logic and then builds a reply.

The split makes failures easier to classify. A wrong answer may come from a wrong intent, missing extracted information, a dialogue transition or the response text, and explicit intermediate results let each be inspected on its own. In the code the dialogue manager returns a dictionary keyed by an action code, and the generation module reads that code, not raw text.

The frontend is a separate Node service built on Botkit. It queues messages per user and schedules the call to the backend about one second after the latest message, cancelling a pending send when another message arrives. It splits the reply on an asterisk into separate chat bubbles and turns the returned options into quick-reply buttons. A docker-compose file starts the two services, the backend on port 8000 and the frontend on port 3000.

sections.title: Clean Vietnamese text before classification
paragraphs: Chat messages in Vietnamese arrive with missing diacritics, Telex typing mistakes, abbreviations and slang. Before any model sees a message, a correction step lowercases it, normalises Unicode, replaces abbreviations and slang from dictionary files, repairs Telex mistakes, and rewrites shorthand such as Q1 into a district name. Punctuation is padded with spaces so the tokens are consistent.

The dictionaries live as JSON and text files in backend/data/spell_corection. Treating them as data instead of code means a new abbreviation can be added without touching the logic. I did not measure how much the correction step improved classification, so the benefit is a design intention and not a result.

sections.title: Use intent models with visible training boundaries
paragraphs: Intent classification uses pickled pairs of a TF-IDF vectorizer and a classifier. Two pairs are loaded at start-up: one for the general intent and one for the sub-intent of a request. The retraining code in backend/api/api_retrain_model.py trains an SVC with a randomized hyperparameter search over C and kernel, ten-fold cross-validation and a ten percent held-out split, and trains a nearest-neighbour model with cosine distance.

The training data for the SVM is read from a MongoDB collection of labelled messages, which also means new examples can be added through an API and the models rebuilt. In the main branch version of the retraining function the SVM call is commented out and only the nearest-neighbour model is rebuilt.

The code prints a training score and a test score, but I found no stored evaluation results, no label counts and no confusion matrix. A training score would not describe conversation quality in any case. A model can classify familiar phrasing well and still fail on short follow-ups, misspellings or requests that overlap several intents. No accuracy figure is claimed here.

sections.title: Entity extraction is rule-based in the repository
paragraphs: In the code I could find, entities are extracted with regular expressions and keyword dictionaries, not with a trained sequence model. Age is a one- or two-digit number in a message that is not also naming a district. Sex comes from two word patterns. Symptoms come from two dictionaries of patterns, one for ordinary symptoms and one for serious ones, and the district comes from a pattern over district names.

That choice fits the domain. The set of things the bot needs is small and fixed, patterns for Vietnamese words with and without diacritics are cheap to write and test, and a match is easy to explain. The cost is coverage: a rephrased symptom or an unusual district spelling is missed unless someone adds a pattern. The extractor also declares a medical-history field that nothing in the code I read fills in.

My portfolio entry for this project also mentions named entity recognition with PhoBERT and CRF. I searched every branch and every commit of the public repository for PhoBERT, CRF and transformer libraries, including the requirements files, and found no training or inference code for such a model. The work may exist elsewhere, but I cannot show it from this repository, so I do not describe it as part of the system here.

sections.title: Let conversation state change the interpretation
paragraphs: The reply pipeline reads the stored turns for the sender, takes the most recent one, and uses its action code as the previous intent and its slots as the starting state. The new entities are then merged in: age, sex and district overwrite earlier values, and symptoms are added as flags. A follow-up such as a single word of agreement is interpreted as an answer to the last question instead of starting from an empty form.

Each turn is stored in MongoDB with the sender, message text, intent, the dialogue result and the reply. That serves two purposes: continuity for the next turn and a record for later model improvement. The current implementation loads every stored turn for the sender and uses only the last, which is simple but would be wasteful for long conversations; I would query for the most recent turn only.

The backend returns a structured response with the reply text, an intent list and any answer options. The options appear only when there is more than one, and the frontend renders them as quick replies. That contract lets the interface present the next step without reconstructing backend decisions from natural language.

sections.title: Four scenarios, four mechanisms
paragraphs: The dialogue manager routes by intent. Each scenario uses the simplest mechanism that fits, and none of them needs open-ended text generation. All reply text is authored: templates stored in MongoDB, formatted with values from the dialogue result.

sections.title: A fixed question tree for symptoms
paragraphs: When a user mentions symptoms, the bot starts a short sequence of yes or no style questions: whether they have been tested, which type of test and the result, whether they have been in an affected area, and whether they have had close contact. The structure is a nested dictionary in diagnose_reply.py, and a counter in the slots records how far along the user is. Unclear answers trigger a repeat of the question with explicit choices as buttons.

The outcomes are three authored response codes named serious, high and low. The bot's own disclaimer text, stored with the replies, says the predictions may be inaccurate and tells users to contact health centres. I have not clinically validated this flow, and the diagram below describes its structure, not medical advice.

sections.title: Answer general questions by retrieval, and ask when unsure
paragraphs: General questions are answered by retrieval, not by classification. The message is vectorised with TF-IDF and compared by cosine distance with a corpus of stored questions. If the closest question is more than 0.85 similar, its stored answer is returned. Otherwise the bot replies with a clarifying prompt that offers the two closest questions as buttons, and a user's choice on the next turn is answered directly.

This is a useful pattern for a narrow domain: a wrong answer delivered confidently costs more than one extra turn. The threshold of 0.85 is a constant in the code and I have no evidence of how it was chosen or tuned. In the refactor branch the question corpus file holds 583 entries; I did not check their coverage or accuracy, and some answers attribute guidance to health authorities that I cannot verify.

flowchart LR
    Q["Question"] --> V["TF-IDF vector"]
    V --> N["Nearest stored questions"]
    N --> T{"Similarity above 0.85"}
    T -- "yes" --> A["Stored answer"]
    T -- "no" --> P["Ask: did you mean one of two"]
    P --> U["User picks a question"]

diagrams.caption: Retrieval flow in common_infor_reply.py. A confident match answers directly; otherwise the user chooses between the two closest stored questions.

code.title: backend/process/DiaglogueManager/utils_message/common_infor_reply.py (abridged)
code.code:
threshold = 0.85
trans = Config.tfidf_knn.transform([text])
distance, idx_choices = Config.model_knn.kneighbors(trans)
distance = 1 - distance[0]
if distance[0] > threshold:
    res_code = 'reply_correct_text'
    choices = [Config.corpus_knn[idx_choices[0][0]]]
else:
    res_code = 'request_correct_text'
    choices = [Config.corpus_knn[i] for i in idx_choices[0]][:2]

sections.title: Limits and what I could not verify
paragraphs: The main branch cannot be run from a clean checkout. The constant definitions module, the trained models and the data directory are git-ignored or tracked through DVC, and the DVC remote is not available to me. Other branches commit pickled models, but I did not run any version. Everything above comes from reading the code, not from executing it.

No evaluation records exist in the repository: no intent accuracy, no retrieval quality, no end-to-end dialogue success rate. There is also no evidence of how many people used the bot, whether it was deployed beyond configuration files for Docker and Heroku, or whether any clinician reviewed the question tree or the answers. I leave those claims out. The system is also tied to a pandemic-era context, and the answers and case-number source would need replacing before any reuse.

sections.title: What the project taught me
paragraphs: A chatbot is a state machine as much as a text generator. Explicit intents, structured extracted information and a separate response contract make its behavior inspectable, and each stage can be tested without the others.

If I rebuilt it, I would keep the stage boundaries and the ask-when-unsure pattern, add a labelled test set for intents and for the retrieval threshold before tuning anything, store evaluation results next to the models, and replace the hand-written patterns for entities with a measured comparison against a trained extractor. The same questions apply to current agent work: which state belongs to this conversation, what does the next action need, and what has actually been persisted? Newer models change the implementation, not the need for clear state and action boundaries.

takeaways: Separating understanding, dialogue management and generation, with explicit intermediate results, makes failures easier to classify.
Retrieval with a similarity threshold and a clarifying question suits a narrow domain better than a confident wrong answer.
Rule-based extraction was simple and explainable but depends on pattern coverage; a trained extractor would need a measured comparison.
Stored conversation state is what turns a follow-up message into an answer, and it doubles as a record for improving the models.
A training score is not a quality measure; the repository has no stored evaluation, so no accuracy is claimed.
